questions.title: How exactly is "1.58 bits" calculated for a ternary weight set \{-1, 0, 1\}?
questions.question_body: The paper states that adding the value 0 to the original binary \{-1, 1\} set results in "1.58 bits." I understand that standard binary is $\log_2(2) = 1$ bit, but I am confused about the math here. Is this simply $\log_2(3)$? If so, why do we describe it as "bits" in the context of storage if hardware typically allocates whole integers (like 2 bits) for three states? Does this imply a specific packing scheme where multiple weights are stored together to achieve this average?

questions.title: Why does the absmean quantization function use a scalar $\gamma$ instead of per-channel scaling?
questions.question_body: In Equation (3), the scaling factor $\gamma$ is defined as the average absolute value of the entire weight matrix ($\frac{1}{nm}\sum_{ij} |W_{ij}|$). Most modern quantization techniques (like per-channel quantization in LLaMA) use a separate scale for each output channel to preserve accuracy. Why does BitNet b1.58 choose a single global scalar for the whole matrix? Doesn't this risk losing significant information in channels with vastly different magnitudes compared to the global average?

questions.title: If weights are ternary, why are activations kept at 8-bit integers instead of 1-bit?
questions.question_body: The abstract mentions that every *parameter* is ternary, but Section 2 clarifies that the model uses "1.58-bit weights and 8-bit activations." Since the main argument of the paper is reducing computation to integer additions, why haven't the authors quantized the activations to 1-bit or ternary as well? Is there a theoretical limitation preventing stable training with 1-bit activations, or is it purely an empirical choice to maintain perplexity scores?

questions.title: How does Straight-Through Estimator (STE) work with the RoundClip function during backpropagation?
questions.question_body: The forward pass uses the non-differentiable `RoundClip` function defined in Equation (2). The paper doesn't explicitly detail the backward pass strategy. Are they using the standard Straight-Through Estimator (STE) where gradients pass through unchanged? If so, given that the weights are clamped strictly to \{-1, 0, 1\}, how do the weights actually update during training? Do they maintain a full-precision shadow copy of weights that gets quantized only during the forward pass, or is there a different mechanism implied by "trained from scratch"?

questions.title: What is the precise relationship between model size and the "crossover point" where b1.58 outperforms FP16?
questions.question_body: The Results section claims that BitNet b1.58 matches FP16 performance starting from a 3B model size, and even outperforms a 3B FP16 model at 3.9B parameters. However, for smaller models (implied <3B), there seems to be a gap. What drives this scaling behavior? Is it that larger matrices allow the statistical approximation of $\gamma$ (the absmean scaler) to become more accurate, thereby mitigating quantization noise? Or does the capacity of larger models simply absorb the information loss better?

questions.title: Does removing biases in LLaMA-alike components negatively impact low-capacity regimes?
questions.question_body: Section 2 mentions adopting LLaMA-alike components which includes removing all biases. While this works well for large FP16 models, bias terms often play a crucial role in stabilizing training for smaller or heavily quantized networks by shifting activation distributions. Given that BitNet b1.58 forces weights into a very discrete space \{-1, 0, 1\}, did the authors experiment with retaining biases? If removed, how does the model compensate for the lack of affine shift flexibility solely through the ternary weights and normalization layers?

questions.title: How is the claimed 71.4x energy saving derived specifically for matrix multiplication?
questions.question_body: In the Energy paragraph, the paper states a 71.4x savings in arithmetic operations energy on 7nm chips based on citations [energycost, pokebnn]. Can someone break down this ratio? I assume it compares one FP16 multiply-add operation against one INT8 addition (since multiplication by -1/0/1 is just sign flipping or zeroing). However, achieving >70x suggests that either FP16 multiplication is incredibly costly relative to INT8 addition on this specific node, or there are secondary factors like memory access energy included in this specific "arithmetic operations" metric that aren't immediately obvious.
